item.title: High-Speed Control of a Fluxonium Qubit via Picosecond Pulses from Josephson Digital Circuits
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Two digital single-flux-quantum (SFQ) protocols manipulate a low-frequency fluxonium qubit: high-frequency flux-packet control delivers an Xπ gate fidelity of 99.995% in 68 ns, while combined quadrature flux-charge control accelerates Xπ to 16.9–27 ns with fidelity >99.99%.

Grade 0.447 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “transmon and fluxonium coherence, single- and two-qubit gate fidelity” · M. V. Bastrakova, D. S. Pashin, V. A. Vozhakov, N. V. Klenov, I. I. Soloviev

Figure

Ground-state population dynamics (a), computational subspace leakage (b), and infidelity 1−F versus drive amplitude (c) for combined flux-charge Xπ gates on three fluxonium parameter sets (gate times 16.9 ns to 27 ns). Leakage stays below 10−4 while infidelity reaches the 10−4 level over a finite drive range.

Asks

Can digital single-flux-quantum circuitry achieve fast, high-fidelity single-qubit control of a fluxonium qubit despite its low transition frequency and stark flux-charge matrix element asymmetry?

But

Numerical multilevel simulations without dissipation, decoherence, timing jitter, or pulse distortion; assumes rectangular SFQ pulses with matched total rotation strengths across quadratures.

Tools

Picosecond SFQ pulse control · Multilevel time-dependent Schrödinger equation solver (10 levels) · Non-destructive-readout (NDRO) digital counter architecture · Independent dual-channel (flux and charge) quadrature pulsing

Abstract

We develop a control strategy for fluxonium qubits based on picosecond single-flux-quantum (SFQ) pulses generated by Josephson digital circuits. A major challenge is that SFQ protocols originally designed for transmon control become inefficient for low-frequency fluxonium. In this regime, the asymmetry of flux and charge couplings leads either to excessive leakage or excessively long gate times. We show that this limitation can be overcome by two complementary protocols. The first protocol employs high-frequency SFQ pulse packets applied through the flux channel, offering a simple, analytically transparent, and robust approach for high-fidelity single-qubit control. The second protocol combines phase-shifted flux and charge pulse sequences to enhance the resonant drive and reduce the gate duration. Multilevel simulations demonstrate single-qubit gate fidelities above 99.99%; the simpler protocol remains robust under moderate variations of qubit parameters and flux bias, while the combined protocol preserves high fidelity while substantially accelerating the gate. These results establish SFQ-based cryogenic control as a realistic route to fast, accurate, and scalable manipulation of fluxonium qubits.

item.title: Implementing rapid reset of superconducting qubits with on-chip dissipation
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Reset time constant median is 48.1 ns with 30 mK effective bath temperature. 400 ns reset pulse brings residual $|e angle$ population from 94.74% down to 0.67% across 20 transmon qubits.

Grade 0.442 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play” · Feiyu Li, Yang Liu, Zhen Yang, Zhenxing Liu, Jiayu Ding, Yang Gao, Xuehui Liang, Weijie Sun, Yanjun Ma, Chuhong Yang, Guangming Xue, He Wang, Fei Yan

Figure

Single-shot readouts in the I-Q plane and cumulative distributions across 20 qubits comparing excited-state populations before and after a 400 ns reset pulse.

Asks

Can on-chip resistive dissipation enable rapid, scalable transmon reset while isolating qubits from thermal noise of external circuitry?

But

Demonstrated across 20 operational qubits measured in four nonadjacent groups on a 72-qubit chip to mitigate crosstalk. Measured median reset time 48.1 ns exceeds the 28.9 ns model prediction, likely due to dephasing and flux-pulse distortion.

Tools

transmon qubits · dedicated λ/4 transmission-line resonators · thin-film PdAu resistive loads · flux-pulsed frequency tuning

Abstract

Rapid and high-fidelity qubit reset is essential for quantum state initialization and quantum error correction. Conventional reset protocols for superconducting qubits often rely on dissipative elements connected to external circuitry, exposing qubits to thermal noise from higher-temperature environments. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a scalable approach to qubit reset and leakage removal over multiple transmon qubits using dedicated dissipation units comprising resonators coupled to on-chip resistive loads. This architecture provides Purcell protection while isolating the qubits from warmer external circuitry. We achieve a median reset time constant of approximately 48 ns for the |g⟩-|e⟩ transition, with an effective bath temperature of 30 mK. A 400-ns reset pulse yields residual excited-state populations of 0.29% and 0.67% for qubits initialized in |g⟩ and |e⟩, respectively. We further demonstrate efficient leakage removal from the |f⟩ state, reducing its residual population to 0.51%. These results establish a simple, reproducible, and easy-to-integrate approach to dissipation engineering in superconducting quantum processors.

item.title: Electrical Stark Tuning and In Situ Field Sensing of V₂ Silicon Vacancies in a 4H-SiC a-Plane Lateral pin-Diode
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Fabricated V2 silicon vacancy qubits in lateral pin-diodes on a-plane 4H-SiC, yielding zero-bias optical linewidths below 80 MHz, in situ local electric-field sensing, and reverse-bias Stark tuning stable over > 4 hours.

Grade 0.435 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Silicon quantum electronics” · Jannik H. Schwarberg (Chair of Electron Devices, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, Erlangen, Germany), Fedor D. Hrunski (Institute of Applied Quantum Technologies, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, Erlangen, Germany), Maximilian Hollendonner (Institute of Applied Quantum Technologies, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, Erlangen, Germany), Wolfgang Knolle (Leibniz-Institut für Oberflächenmodifizierung, Leipzig, Germany), Mathias Rommel (Fraunhofer Institute for Integrated Systems and Device Technology IISB, Erlangen, Germany), Fabian J. Magerl (Chair of Electron Devices, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, Erlangen, Germany), Jan F. Dick (Chair of Electron Devices, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, Erlangen, Germany, Fraunhofer Institute for Integrated Systems and Device Technology IISB, Erlangen, Germany), Jörg Schulze (Chair of Electron Devices, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, Erlangen, Germany, Fraunhofer Institute for Integrated Systems and Device Technology IISB, Erlangen, Germany)

Asks

Can V2 silicon vacancies in lateral pin-diodes on a-plane 4H-SiC provide surface optical addressability and stable electrical Stark tuning after CMOS processing?

But

Cryogenic temperatures; requires relaxation period to eliminate initial transient charge fluctuations before achieving 4-hour spectral stability.

Tools

a-plane 4H-SiC lateral pin-diode · CMOS-compatible processing · Stark effect optical spectroscopy · cryogenic confocal microscopy · TCAD device simulations

Abstract

Silicon carbide has emerged as a highly promising platform for scalable quantum technologies, with the silicon vacancy serving as a robust spin qubit and quantum sensor. However, conventional c-plane 4H-SiC restricts the experimental scheme and resonant optical excitation to the sample's geometry. The usage of a-plane substrates enables more versatile resonant optical access to the color center through the wafer surface. Here, we demonstrate the electrical control and optical addressability of V₂ (cubic lattice site) silicon vacancies within the intrinsic region of lateral pin-diodes fabricated on a-plane 4H-SiC wafers using a scalable complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) process. Despite extensive semiconductor processing, the integrated color centers exhibit good optical quality, evidenced by narrow optical transition linewidths below 80 MHz at zero bias. These embedded quantum sensors are utilized for in situ measurement of local electric fields at cryogenic temperatures via the Stark effect. Comparisons with macroscopic technology computer-aided design simulations reveal the value of these integrated quantum sensors to help understand cryogenic device behavior, for example in predicting highly localized field crowding. Furthermore, to address the spectral indistinguishability required for quantum networks, we precisely tune the zero-phonon line (ZPL) of individual emitters via the reverse-bias Stark effect. This successfully compensates for the spectral variations of distinct emitters. Following the relaxation of transient charge fluctuations, the Stark-tuned emitters exhibit spectral stability over measurement periods exceeding four hours. Our results establish a-plane 4H-SiC as a robust platform for future interference experiments and quantum photonic integrated circuits.

item.title: Field-induced phase-matching in Josephson traveling wave parametric amplifiers
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Phase-matching in a homogeneous 912-SNAIL JTWPA achieved without integrated resonators by exploiting coil field inhomogeneity and flux focusing, producing broadband 3-wave mixing gain across 4 GHz−8 GHz for Φ≳6Φ0 with a 12 GHz pump.

Grade 0.429 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Charge-insensitive qubit design derived from the Cooper pair box” · Daniil E. Bazulin, Simon Gandorfer, Niklas Bruckmoser, Kedar E. Honasoge, Leon Koch, Maria-Teresa Handschuh, Matthias Hirschbichler, Kirill Shulga, Achim Marx, Michael Haider, Stefan Filipp, Kirill G. Fedorov

Figure

Normalized transmission gain as a function of signal frequency and external flux Φ for pump frequencies of 10, 11, and 12 GHz, showing experimental measurements alongside three-mode and multi-mode simulations that capture the pump-frequency-dependent flux threshold Φt for broadband gain emergence.

Asks

Can an inhomogeneous external magnetic field provide phase-matching in a uniform Josephson traveling wave parametric amplifier without on-chip resonant structures?

But

Measurements conducted at 15 mK; requires sufficiently large magnetic flux offsets Φ≫Φ0; gain onset is sensitive to the spatial profile of the magnetic field distribution along the meandered array.

Tools

912-SNAIL chain · double-mask Manhattan-style overlap Josephson junctions · dilution refrigerator at 15mK · vector network analyzer · multi-mode harmonic balance model

Abstract

Superconducting Josephson traveling wave parametric amplifiers (JTWPAs) enable broadband, quantum-limited amplification of weak microwave signals. JTWPAs are essential for the single-shot readout of superconducting qubits, broadband vacuum squeezing, or the generation of microwave cluster states. Phase-matching between signal and pump modes in such JTWPAs represents a major engineering challenge, which is typically solved by integrating resonators in a nonlinear medium in order to tailor electromagnetic dispersion relations and achieve a broadband, high-gain amplification. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a phase-matching approach using a homogeneous nonlinear medium based on Josephson elements by exploiting a magnetic field inhomogeneity. We show how the latter may lead to the sign reversal of the 3-wave mixing nonlinearity and stabilization of the parametric amplification. We envision this technique as a viable alternative to conventional phase-matching approaches.

item.title: Long-range correlated quantum errors from diffuson-correlated dephasing
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Disorder-induced soft modes (diffusons) in shared conductors impose dephasing correlations scaling as ηij≈−cos⁡(ϕi+ϕj)/n2. Worst-case integrated correlated noise per qubit grows as 2ln⁡min⁡(N,Dt/Lq2), violating the standard fault-tolerance threshold condition in two dimensions.

Grade 0.427 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · N. R. S. van Venrooij, M. E. Flatté

Figure

Summed pair correlations 𝒮 for three co-aligned qubits in a triangular geometry at dipole angles ϕ=0∘ and ϕ=60∘, demonstrating that spatial dephasing shifts between correlated and anti-correlated regimes depending purely on orientation.

Asks

What is the spatial structure and array-size scaling of dephasing noise mediated between solid-state qubits by low-energy collective modes in a shared disordered conductor?

But

Truncated at Gaussian order in charge-density fluctuations. Evaluates disorder-averaged kernel without sample-specific mesoscopic fluctuations or weak-localization corrections from Cooperons. Worst-case scaling assumes absolute value sum without dynamical phase cancellation.

Tools

Keldysh nonlinear sigma model · saddle-point analysis · disorder averaging

Abstract

Electrical solid-state qubits are generally initialized, manipulated and read out through diffusive conductors. We show that the disorder-induced low energy modes of such a conductor --- diffusons --- impose spatially correlated dephasing on any qubits that share it, a mechanism we term diffuson-correlated dephasing. Starting from a Keldysh nonlinear sigma model for the disordered conductive region, coupled capacitively to two-level systems, we obtain the noise kernel in closed form. It decays as the inverse square of the qubit separation and changes sign with the orientation of the pair, so that qubit pairs at equal separation may be correlated or anticorrelated, an unambiguous experimental signature. In two dimensions, the correlated noise a single qubit shares with the rest of the array, in the worst-case scenario, grows logarithmically with array size rather than converging. The sufficient condition for fault tolerance under correlated noise is therefore violated, so standard threshold theorems no longer guarantee protection against this channel for large qubit arrays. As this dephasing originates from the soft-mode content of the environment rather than on any specific gate detail, we expect correlated dephasing channels of this kind wherever solid-state qubits or sensors share a gapless conductive medium.

item.title: Double-quantum enhanced coherent control and magnetic sensing of spin defects in hexagonal boron nitride
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Double-quantum driving of VB− ground-state manifold enhances optical readout contrast and yields 2.6-fold signal-to-noise improvement in AC magnetometry over single-quantum protocols.

Grade 0.417 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Shihao Ru, Abdullah Rasmita, Jiakai Chen, Yuzhe Yang, Xiaodan Lyu, Robert Cernansky, Edwin Hang Tong Teo, Jesús Zúñiga-Pérez, Fedor Jelezko, Weibo Gao

Asks

Can coherent control of the Δms=2 double-quantum transition in VB− ensembles enhance magnetic sensitivity and isolate local electric/strain noise sources in hBN?

Before

Standard hBN spin sensing probed single-quantum transitions separately with lower signal-to-noise ratio.

But

Demonstrated on an ensemble in hBN; noise source discrimination depends on assumed models for correlated-surface versus volume-distributed fluctuations.

Tools

negatively charged boron vacancies (V_B⁻) · hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) spin ensemble · simultaneous two-tone microwave resonant driving · optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) · AC magnetometry

Abstract

The negatively charged boron vacancy (V_B⁻) in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is a promising spin defect for quantum sensing in two-dimensional material systems. Previous hBN experiments have mainly exploited the two spin-triplet ground-state single-quantum transitions separately. Here we implement a double-quantum driving scheme based on simultaneous resonant microwave excitation of both ground-state single-quantum transitions, establishing coherent control of the Δm_s=2 manifold in a V_B⁻ ensemble. We compare the resulting double-quantum response with the corresponding single-quantum protocol under identical experimental conditions. The double-quantum protocol enhances the optical readout contrast and yields a 2.6-fold signal-to-noise improvement in AC magnetometry. We further use the double-quantum relaxation channel as a differential probe of electric-field and strain noise, showing that the present data are compatible with correlated-surface or volume-distributed fluctuations, while short-range uncorrelated surface-noise models are disfavored within the assumptions of our analysis. These results establish double-quantum coherent control and frequency-resolved AC magnetometry in hBN spin ensembles, and identify the sample-dependent measurements needed to determine the microscopic origin of the dominant relaxation channels.

item.arxave:tools: negatively charged boron vacancies (V_B⁻) · hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) spin ensemble · simultaneous two-tone microwave resonant driving · optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) · AC magnetometry
item.arxave:abstract: The negatively charged boron vacancy (V_B⁻) in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is a promising spin defect for quantum sensing in two-dimensional material systems. Previous hBN experiments have mainly exploited the two spin-triplet ground-state single-quantum transitions separately. Here we implement a double-quantum driving scheme based on simultaneous resonant microwave excitation of both ground-state single-quantum transitions, establishing coherent control of the Δm_s=2 manifold in a V_B⁻ ensemble. We compare the resulting double-quantum response with the corresponding single-quantum protocol under identical experimental conditions. The double-quantum protocol enhances the optical readout contrast and yields a 2.6-fold signal-to-noise improvement in AC magnetometry. We further use the double-quantum relaxation channel as a differential probe of electric-field and strain noise, showing that the present data are compatible with correlated-surface or volume-distributed fluctuations, while short-range uncorrelated surface-noise models are disfavored within the assumptions of our analysis. These results establish double-quantum coherent control and frequency-resolved AC magnetometry in hBN spin ensembles, and identify the sample-dependent measurements needed to determine the microscopic origin of the dominant relaxation channels.
